Updates cspell from 10.3.2 to 10.3.3

Release notes

Sourced from cspell's releases.

v10.3.3

Fixes

fix: Add --json option to check text for use with AI (#9254)

This pull request adds support for a --json output mode to the check CLI command, enabling results to be emitted as structured JSON per file. It also introduces comprehensive test coverage for the new JSON output behavior, including error handling and exit code logic.

CLI Enhancements:

  • Added a --json flag to the check command, allowing users to receive results in JSON format. This includes proper handling of multiple files and error cases, such as missing files. [1] [2]
  • Updated the exit code logic to work with both standard and JSON output, respecting the --no-exit-code flag. [1] [2]

Implementation Details:

  • Introduced separate processing functions: processRequestAnsi for standard output and processRequestJSON for JSON output, with the latter aggregating results and errors per file. [1] [2]
  • Added a helper function to detect missing files and report them as JSON errors.

Testing Improvements:

  • Expanded CLI test coverage to include various --json scenarios, such as files with spelling errors, missing files, and the interaction with --no-exit-code. [1] [2]
  • Added utility functions and interfaces in tests to parse and validate the JSON output.

fix: Mark ParsedTags as read only. (#9253)

This pull request makes a small but important change to the ParsedText interface in several files, improving type safety by marking the tags property as a read-only type. This ensures that the tags associated with a parsed text segment cannot be modified after creation.

  • Updated the tags property in the ParsedText interface to use Readonly<ParsedTags> instead of ParsedTags, making the tags immutable in the following files:
    • packages/cspell-types/api/Parser/index.d.mts
    • packages/cspell-types/api/index.d.mts
    • packages/cspell-types/src/Parser/parser.ts

fix: Make sure Parser and DocumentParser can be used together. (#9252)

This pull request enhances the parser interface definitions in the cspell-types package to provide better flexibility and clarity for parser implementations. The main changes introduce optional parseDocument and parse methods to both the Parser and DocumentParser interfaces, across both type declaration and source files.

items.content_html:
Description

Adds a "Dictionary freshness" section to the Compression Dictionary Transport guide and a one-sentence pointer on the Use-As-Dictionary reference page.

RFC 9842 §2.2.1 says a dictionary "MUST be either fresh or allowed to be served stale (see RFC 5861)" to be considered as a match. Neither MDN page mentions it: the guide covers caching only for Vary and cache partitioning, and the reference page does not mention Cache-Control at all. In practice that one sentence decides whether a dictionary is stored, and the consequences are not obvious from it, so the section spells them out:

  • no-cache, no-store and must-revalidate each stop a response being used as a dictionary, whatever else the header carries.
  • max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=N registers, and N is the dictionary's lifetime.
  • s-maxage is invisible, since the browser is a private cache.

Measured in Chrome (one navigation per policy, watching whether the next matching request carried Available-Dictionary):

Cache-Control on the offering response registers
max-age=3600 yes
max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=604800 yes
public, max-age=0, s-maxage=86400, stale-while-revalidate=604800 yes
public, max-age=0, s-maxage=86400, stale-while-revalidate=5 no (usable for 5 seconds)
max-age=0, must-revalidate no
max-age=0, must-revalidate, stale-while-revalidate=604800 no
private, no-cache, must-revalidate no
private, no-cache, stale-while-revalidate=604800 no

The reason it earns a section rather than a footnote is that the failure is silent: the header is accepted, nothing is reported to the page, and the next request just carries no Available-Dictionary. It is easy to ship a whole page-dictionary tier that never matches, because HTML documents are commonly served with no-cache or must-revalidate. The section names the DevTools message that explains it ("The response can't be used as a dictionary because its freshness is expired").

Motivation

Hit this on a site that offers each page as a dictionary for its next version. The document tier had been served must-revalidate and every offer was being dropped; nothing in the docs or the spec's own text pointed at the cache headers.

Additional details

RFC 9842 §2.2.1: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9842#section-2.2.1

Related issues and pull requests

None found.
items.title: Document dictionary freshness for Compression Dictionary Transport

items.content_html:
Description

outline and outline-color both carry an Accessibility section. outline-offset does not, even though it is the property in that family that decides whether a focus indicator can be seen at all.

Adds one section covering the two things the offset changes about a focus indicator:

  • Which background the contrast ratio is measured against. The page already notes that the space the offset creates is transparent, so the outline is drawn over whatever is behind the element rather than over the element. That means the 3:1 required by SC 1.4.11 is measured against that background, and a negative offset moves the outline inside the border edge, over the element's own background, where the answer can differ.
  • Whether the indicator survives clipping. A positive offset can move the outline outside an ancestor that clips overflow, or outside a scroll container, cutting part of it off. That is the practical case behind SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), and SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance sets a minimum area for the indicator.

Placed after Description and before Formal definition, matching where outline-color puts its own Accessibility section.

Motivation

The existing Description explains the mechanism (the gap is transparent) without saying what follows from it for a focus style, which is the main reason authors set this property. Both consequences are commonly missed, and the clipping one is invisible until someone tabs through a scrolling region.
items.title: docs(css): add an Accessibility section to outline-offset

items.content_html:
Description

The Accessibility section of outline-color states the requirements for text contrast on a property that colors an outline. An outline is a user interface component, not text, so Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) does not apply to it. The applicable criterion is 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, which requires 3:1.

The current wording is also actively misleading in two ways:

  • It tells the reader an outline needs 4.5:1, which overstates the requirement.
  • It offers the large-text exemption ("3:1 for larger text such as headings", "18.66px and bold or larger"), which has no meaning for an outline and could be read as licence to use 3:1 only in some cases. For non-text contrast, 3:1 is the requirement in all cases.

MDN already documents this correctly on the two pages a reader is most likely to arrive from: :focus and :focus-visible both cite SC 1.4.11 and 3:1. This change removes the contradiction.

The replacement paragraph also notes that a focus outline may border both the page background and the element's own background, so both count as adjacent colors. That follows from the "adjacent colors" wording in 1.4.11 and is the case authors most often get wrong.

The stale reference to the WCAG 2.0 Understanding document for SC 1.4.3 is replaced with the WCAG 2.2 Understanding document for SC 1.4.11.

Motivation

An author following this page today can ship a focus indicator built to the wrong criterion, and will get a different answer from this page than from the :focus page.

Single file, single section, no change to the first paragraph or to the two remaining links.
items.title: fix(css): outline contrast is governed by SC 1.4.11, not text contrast

items.content_html:
The Attestation section said keys come from a specific device and that validating the root of trust is frequently unnecessary, both contradicted by the WebAuthn spec: attestation identifies a device model or batch, and verification is what proves a self-contained multi-factor credential. This replaces the paragraph with the spec-cited wording from the issue.

One paragraph, nothing else.

Closes #45753

Verification

  • Checked each claim against the cited W3C WebAuthn-3 sections in the issue
  • No trailing whitespace; front matter untouched
items.title: Correct the WebAuthn attestation purpose paragraph
